title: Universal Properties, Representables and the Yoneda Lemma

items.title: The covariant and contravariant hom-assignments and the hom-bifunctor of a locally small category
The assignments $\mathcal C(a,-)$ and $\mathcal C(-,a)$ are functors to $\mathbf{Set}$
items.strategy: For a morphism $u:b\to c$, define the covariant action by postcomposition $f\mapsto u\circ f$ and the contravariant action by precomposition $g\mapsto g\circ u$. Associativity gives preservation of composition, and the identity laws give preservation of identities.

items.title: The hom-assignment $\mathcal C(-,-):\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C\to\mathbf{Set}$ is a bifunctor
items.strategy: Send $(h:a'\to a,u:b\to b')$ to $f\mapsto u\circ f\circ h$. Check identity and composition componentwise; associativity also shows that precomposition and postcomposition commute, so the two one-variable hom-functors assemble into one bifunctor.

items.title: Presheaves, covariantly and contravariantly representable functors, and representations
Initial and terminal objects are exactly the representations of the constant singleton functor
items.strategy: For the covariant case, a representation $\mathcal C(I,-)\cong 1$ says that every hom-set out of $I$ is a singleton, exactly the initial-object condition. Apply the same argument to $\mathcal C(-,T)\cong1$ for terminal objects, including the empty-category obstruction.

items.title: Initial and terminal objects are unique up to a unique isomorphism
items.strategy: Between two initial objects there is one morphism in each direction. Each composite is an endomorphism of an initial object and hence must be its unique endomorphism, the identity; uniqueness of the isomorphism follows from uniqueness of the forward morphism. Dualize for terminal objects.

items.title: Evaluation at the identity gives $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(a,-),F)\cong F(a)$ and proves that the natural-transformation collection is a set
items.strategy: Define evaluation by $\alpha\mapsto\alpha_a(1_a)$. For $x\in F(a)$ construct $\alpha^x_c(f)=F(f)(x)$, check naturality, and prove the two constructions inverse using the naturality square for $f:a\to c$. Only after this explicit bijection is constructed identify the natural-transformation collection with a set; no choice is used.

items.title: The Yoneda bijection $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(a,-),F)\cong F(a)$ is natural in both $a$ and $F$
items.strategy: Use the explicit evaluation bijection. For $h:a\to a'$, verify that precomposition with $\mathcal C(h,-):\mathcal C(a',-)\Rightarrow\mathcal C(a,-)$ corresponds to $F(h)$; for $\eta:F\Rightarrow G$, verify that postcomposition by $\eta$ corresponds to $\eta_a$. These two equations establish the two naturality squares without assuming a functor category for a large source.

items.title: For a presheaf $P$, $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(-,a),P)\cong P(a)$ naturally in $a$ and $P$
items.strategy: Apply the covariant Yoneda lemma to $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}$. Translate its covariant hom-functor, object morphisms, and naturality equations back to the stated presheaf variance.

items.title: Local smallness does not make every natural-transformation collection a set, but the Yoneda construction proves sethood in the representable-source case
The Yoneda assignment and the small-source Yoneda functor, traditionally called the Yoneda embedding
The Yoneda functor is fully faithful, and it is a full embedding when its object map is injective
items.strategy: Specialize contravariant Yoneda to $P=\mathcal C(-,b)$ to obtain $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(-,a),\mathcal C(-,b))\cong\mathcal C(a,b)$. Check that the inverse sends $f:a\to b$ to postcomposition by $f$, exactly the morphism action of $y$; the bijection gives fullness and faithfulness with no global smallness needed for the hom-set claim. Under the library's stronger terminology, add the conditional object-injectivity clause before calling this a full embedding.

items.title: Objects $a$ and $b$ are isomorphic exactly when $\mathcal C(-,a)$ and $\mathcal C(-,b)$ are naturally isomorphic
items.strategy: An isomorphism $a\to b$ is sent by Yoneda to a natural isomorphism. Conversely, full faithfulness lifts a natural isomorphism and its inverse to morphisms $a\to b$ and $b\to a$; faithfulness turns the two inverse equations into the corresponding equations in $\mathcal C$.

items.title: Universal elements of covariant functors and presheaves
A representation is equivalently a universal element with a unique factorisation property
items.strategy: For covariant $F$, send a representation $\theta:\mathcal C(R,-)\cong F$ to $u=\theta_R(1_R)$ and use Yoneda's inverse formula to show $\theta_c(f)=F(f)(u)$. Conversely the stipulated unique factorization makes each such map bijective, and functoriality makes the family natural. Apply the dual argument to presheaves.

items.title: Representing objects are unique up to a unique isomorphism compatible with their universal elements
items.strategy: Given universal elements $(R,u)$ and $(R',u')$ for the same covariant functor, use universality to obtain the unique maps $i:R\to R'$ and $j:R'\to R$ carrying one universal element to the other. Functoriality and uniqueness force $ji=1_R$ and $ij=1_{R'}$, and also force uniqueness of the compatible isomorphism; dualize for presheaves.

items.title: The category of elements of a covariant functor or a presheaf
Universal elements are initial in a covariant category of elements and terminal in a presheaf category of elements
items.strategy: Unpack a morphism $(R,u)\to(c,x)$ in the covariant category of elements: it is exactly a morphism $f:R\to c$ satisfying $F(f)(u)=x$, so initiality is precisely the universal-factorization condition. The presheaf equation reverses the arrow and yields terminality.

items.title: Universal arrows from an object to a functor and from a functor to an object
Universal arrows to a functor are initial in comma categories, and universal arrows from a functor are terminal
items.strategy: An arrow in $(X\downarrow U)$ from $(R,\eta)$ to $(C,f)$ is a morphism $h:R\to C$ with $U(h)\eta=f$, exactly the unique factorization in a universal arrow from $X$ to $U$. Unpack $(U\downarrow X)$ dually for universal arrows from $U$ to $X$.

title: Universal Properties, Representables and the Yoneda Lemma — Examples

items.title: A Cartesian product represents $X\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X,A)\times\mathbf{Set}(X,B)$
items.strategy: Use $A\times B$ with its projections. Send $f:X\to A\times B$ to its two coordinate maps, send a pair $(g,h)$ to $x\mapsto(g(x),h(x))$, and check that these operations are inverse and natural in $X$.

items.title: A tagged disjoint union represents $X\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(A,X)\times\mathbf{Set}(B,X)$
items.strategy: Construct $A\sqcup B=(A\times\{0\})\cup(B\times\{1\})$. Restriction along the two injections sends a map out of the union to a pair of maps; define the inverse piecewise on the two tags and verify uniqueness and naturality.

items.title: The function set $B^A$ represents $X\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X\times A,B)$
items.strategy: Curry a map $f:X\times A\to B$ to $x\mapsto(a\mapsto f(x,a))$ and uncurry a map $X\to B^A$ by evaluation. The two formulas are inverse and commute with precomposition in $X$.

items.title: The free word monoid on $X$ represents $M\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X,U(M))$
items.strategy: Form the monoid $X^*$ of finite words under concatenation and the one-letter map $j:X\to X^*$. Extend $f:X\to U(M)$ to the product of the letters in a word, prove this is the unique unital monoid homomorphism extending $f$, and check naturality in $M$. Also verify that monoids and unital homomorphisms form a locally small category and that $U$ is a functor.

items.title: The free group on $X$ represents $G\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X,U(G))$
items.strategy: Apply the published free-group universal property to obtain a bijection $\mathbf{Grp}(F(X),G)\cong\mathbf{Set}(X,U(G))$. Show that postcomposition by a group homomorphism agrees with postcomposition of the underlying set map, proving naturality; for a singleton $X$, identify $F(X)$ with the infinite cyclic group.

items.title: $\mathbb Z[x]$ represents the underlying-set functor on unital rings
items.strategy: For an arbitrary unital ring $R$ and $r\in R$, define evaluation by $\sum_i a_i x^i\mapsto\sum_i(a_i1_R)r^i$. Integer scalars are central, so the convolution calculation proves multiplicativity without assuming $R$ commutative. Show that every unital homomorphism $\mathbb Z[x]\to R$ is forced by the image of $x$, and verify naturality under postcomposition.

items.title: The one-point space represents the underlying-set functor on $\mathbf{Top}$
items.strategy: A map from the one-point space $1$ to $X$ is determined by its unique image point, and every such map is continuous because each preimage is either empty or all of $1$. This gives $\mathbf{Top}(1,X)\cong U(X)$, naturally under continuous maps.

items.title: A representable presheaf on a poset is the indicator of a principal down-set
items.strategy: View a poset $P$ as a category and fix $p\in P$. Compute $P(-,p)$ at $q$: it is a singleton when $q\le p$ and empty otherwise. The unique possible restriction maps display the presheaf completely and identify its nonempty support with the principal down-set of $p$.

items.title: The functor $D(X)=X\sqcup X$ on $\mathbf{Set}$ is not covariantly representable
items.strategy: Define $D$ on a function by applying it separately to the two tags. If $D\cong\mathbf{Set}(R,-)$, evaluation at a singleton would give a bijection from the two-element set $D(1)$ to the singleton $\mathbf{Set}(R,1)$, an immediate contradiction for every set $R$.

items.title: Two singleton sets give canonically isomorphic representations of the identity functor on $\mathbf{Set}$
items.strategy: Represent the identity functor by $\{0\}$ and by $\{1\}$ through evaluation at the unique point. The unique bijection $\{0\}\to\{1\}$ is the unique isomorphism carrying one universal point to the other, illustrating compatibility rather than merely an arbitrary isomorphism.

items.title: The Yoneda embedding of the walking-arrow category computed objectwise
items.strategy: For the category $0\xrightarrow{u}1$, tabulate $y(0)$ and $y(1)$ on both objects and on $u^{\mathrm{op}}$, then compute $y(u):y(0)\Rightarrow y(1)$. The resulting natural-transformation sets reproduce the three hom-sets and their composition.

items.title: For a monoid action, Yoneda says that an equivariant map from the regular action is determined by the identity element
items.strategy: View a monoid $M$ as its one-object category and a functor $BM\to\mathbf{Set}$ as a left $M$-set $X$. Identify $BM(*,-)$ with the left regular action on $M$; evaluation at the identity sends an equivariant map $M\to X$ to a point of $X$, with inverse $x\mapsto(m\mapsto m\cdot x)$.

items.title: The Yoneda lemma requires its category to be small
items.strategy: Refute the claim by the proved theorem: its construction uses only that each $\mathcal C(a,c)$ is a set. The large locally small category $\mathbf{Set}$ supplies a concrete category outside the small case, while the same evaluation-and-inverse formulas still apply.

items.title: Non-isomorphic objects can have naturally isomorphic representable presheaves
items.strategy: A natural isomorphism $\mathcal C(-,a)\cong\mathcal C(-,b)$ lifts by full faithfulness to mutually inverse morphisms $a\to b$ and $b\to a$. This contradicts non-isomorphism and directly refutes the claim.
